Moringa.name: Moringa Pod Fly (Gitona distigma)
Moringa.description: Major dipteran pest where maggots feed inside tender pods causing internal rotting, gum exudation, and drying.
symptoms: Oozing of gummy liquid from small punctures on tender pods
Drying and splitting of immature pods from the tip
Premature drop of young pods and internal pulp rotting
Small white maggots visible inside split pods upon dissection
risk_conditions: Warm humid weather during pod formation
Unharvested rotten pods left hanging or on the basin floor
Continuous flowering and fruiting cycles without orchard cleanup
monitoring: Inspect 20 random pod clusters weekly across the orchard during pod set
Install methyl eugenol or fermented jaggery bait traps at 4–5 traps per acre
Check for gum droplets on young pods measuring 10–25 cm in length
prevention: Maintain clean basin sanitation by removing and burying dropped and rotten pods deeply
Avoid overlapping unpruned old branches that harbor puparia in the soil
Deep summer ploughing or basin raking to expose pupae to solar heat and predatory birds
cultural_control: Prompt collection and burning or deep pit-burial of infested pods
Prune trees immediately after peak harvest to break the reproductive cycle
Intercrop with non-host flowering crops like marigold to harbor natural parasitoids
mechanical_control: Bagging of young pod clusters with breathable mesh bags in small-scale cultivation
Erect yellow sticky traps and poison bait traps to capture adult flies
biological_control: Conservation of pupal parasitoids like Spalangia endius and Opius spp.
Soil application of entomopathogenic nematodes (Heterorhabditis spp.) targeting pupating larvae

active_ingredients: Azadirachtin (Neem seed kernel extract 5% / EC formulations)
Spinosad (where recommended by local extension for severe borer pressure)
chemical_control.target: Adult pod flies during early pod initiation before maggots enter the fruit tissue
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Consider botanical or approved selective intervention only if pod oozing exceeds 10% of sampled clusters.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Do not spray broad-spectrum insecticides during peak blooming to safeguard pollinating bees. Follow current locally approved CIBRC/TNAU label guidelines.

severity_levels.description: Less than 5% young pods show isolated gum droplets; no widespread pod drying.
5% to 15% pods exhibit gum oozing and localized terminal drying.
More than 15% pods damaged with severe rotting, premature drop, and abundant fly activity.

Moringa.name: Moringa Hairy Caterpillar (Eupterote mollifera / Streblote siva)
Moringa.description: Defoliating pest where hairy caterpillars congregate in dense colonies on tree trunks during daytime and defoliate branches at night.
symptoms: Dense masses of hairy caterpillars clustered together on tree trunks and main forks
Severe defoliation of leaves leaving bare branches
Presence of bristly urticating hairs causing irritation on skin contact
Faecal pellets accumulating beneath the tree canopy
risk_conditions: Post-monsoon warm, humid weather (August to December in South India)
Overgrown, dense tree canopies with unmanaged weeds around tree bases
monitoring: Examine tree trunks, main branch forks, and soil collar weekly for caterpillar clusters
Check for fresh green leaf fragments and droppings on the basin ground
Monitor light traps for adult nocturnal moth activity
prevention: Regular weed clearance and basin hoeing around tree trunks
Deep summer ploughing to expose pupae in the soil to solarization and predators
Prune dead and excessively dense inner branches to maximize sunlight penetration
cultural_control: Band tree trunks with smooth plastic sheets or grease barriers to impede upward caterpillar migration
Mechanically crush or collect congregating colonies using a torch or kerosene-water container during daytime
mechanical_control: Hand-collect egg masses and early-instar caterpillar clusters on lower branches using protective gloves
Operate light traps (1 trap per hectare) to attract and destroy adult female moths
biological_control: Conservation of tachinid fly and braconid wasp larval parasitoids
Foliar application of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or Beauveria bassiana targeting early instars

active_ingredients: Neem oil / Azadirachtin formulations
Contact botanical or approved contact sprays directed strictly onto trunk clusters
chemical_control.target: Congregated caterpillar colonies on trunk bark before they disperse to upper foliage
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Spot-treat clustered colonies on the trunk when aggregations are spotted before significant defoliation occurs.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Wear protective gloves and eye gear to prevent skin irritation from stinging hairs. Direct sprays only at trunk aggregations rather than whole-canopy spraying.

severity_levels.description: Isolated small clusters on 1–2 tree trunks; leaf damage under 10%.
Multiple colonies per tree; 10% to 25% leaf loss with active nighttime feeding.
Complete defoliation of several trees; heavy mass congregations on all main trunks.

Moringa.name: Root & Collar Rot (Fusarium spp. / Rhizoctonia solani)
Moringa.description: Fungal complex attacking collar region and roots under waterlogged or poor drainage conditions, causing wilting and tree collapse.
symptoms: Yellowing and sudden wilting of foliage across one branch or the entire canopy
Dark brown to black discoloration and softening of the collar region near soil line
Peeling of root bark with foul odor and decay of feeder roots
Loosening of the tree in soil, easily toppled by wind
risk_conditions: Heavy clay soils with poor internal drainage or prolonged water ponding
Excessive irrigation around trunk basins without ridge planting
Physical wounds on collar caused during weeding or intercultural operations
monitoring: Check tree collar lines weekly after irrigation or heavy rains for bark softening
Observe yellowing leaves that fail to revive after standard irrigation
Inspect root collar zone if young trees exhibit branch dieback
prevention: Plant on raised beds or broad ridges with dedicated drainage furrows
Avoid stagnant water contact with the tree trunk using ring-and-basin irrigation
Enrich planting pits with well-rotted FYM fortified with Trichoderma harzianum
cultural_control: Remove and burn dead or collapsed trees including root stumps to prevent mycelial spread
Scrape slightly infected collar bark and expose the collar region to sunlight to dry
Apply neem cake blended with Trichoderma around the basin zone
mechanical_control: Excavate drainage channels to rapidly discharge excess monsoon runoff away from tree basins
Avoid mechanical injury to trunk base during weeding tools operation
biological_control: Trichoderma viride or Trichoderma harzianum soil drenching and root-basin application
Pseudomonas fluorescens root-zone soil application with compost

active_ingredients: Copper oxychloride (protective collar drench)
Bordeaux paste (for application onto scraped trunk lesions)
chemical_control.target: Collar region and surrounding soil in newly affected and neighboring healthy trees
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Apply protective copper-based drench at initial wilting symptoms or after prolonged flooding.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Ensure drenched liquid reaches the root zone around the collar. Follow statutory safety intervals and locally approved labels.

severity_levels.description: Slight yellowing of outer branch tips; collar bark intact and firm.
Noticeable collar discoloration on 10–20% of trees with partial leaf shed.
Complete collar rot, bark sloughing, and sudden tree wilting across multiple trees.

Paddy.name: Yellow Stem Borer (Scirpophaga incertulas)
Paddy.description: Monophagous pest where larvae bore inside the tillers causing 'deadheart' at vegetative stage and 'white ear' at heading stage.
symptoms: 'Deadheart' - central vegetative shoots dry up and can be pulled out easily with severed base
'White ear' - bleached, empty erect panicles with no grain filling during reproductive stage
Small exit and entrance pinholes on lower stem nodes
Buff-colored egg masses covered with yellowish-brown silky anal hairs on upper leaf tips
risk_conditions: High nitrogen fertilizer application exceeding recommended doses
Staggered planting across adjacent fields creating continuous host presence
Warm, humid weather with overcast skies and high night temperatures
monitoring: Scout 20 hill clusters diagonally across the field twice a week
Install light traps (1 trap/acre) and sex pheromone traps (3–4 traps/acre) to monitor moth flights
Economic Threshold Level (ETL): 1 egg mass/sq.m or 2 moths/trap/day or 10% deadhearts / 2% white ears
prevention: Synchronous community transplanting across contiguous field blocks
Clip leaf tips of seedlings before transplanting to eliminate attached egg masses
Adopt balanced nitrogen application split into 3–4 timings rather than heavy basal doses
cultural_control: Harvest rice plants at ground level and plough stubbles immediately to expose diapausing larvae
Alternate wetting and moderate drying irrigation rather than continuous deep flooding
Allow predatory ducks or birds into fields during fallow and early tillering
mechanical_control: Hand-collection and destruction of egg masses from nursery and early transplanted fields
Erect T-shaped bird perches at 15–20 per acre for insectivorous birds like drongos
biological_control: Release egg parasitoid Trichogramma japonicum at weekly intervals starting 30 days after transplanting
Conservation of spiders (Lycosa pseudoannulata), mirid bugs, and carabid ground beetles

active_ingredients: Neem formulation (Azadirachtin)
Cartap hydrochloride / Chlorantraniliprole (where ETL is exceeded under official guidance)
chemical_control.target: Newly hatched young larvae before they bore completely into the interior of the culm
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Apply intervention only when moth catches or deadhearts exceed established Economic Threshold Levels.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Avoid spraying if predator spider population is high. Maintain water level for 24–48 hours post application according to label instructions.

severity_levels.description: Under 5% deadhearts at vegetative stage; isolated egg masses observed.
5% to 10% deadhearts or active pheromone trap catches crossing ETL.
Over 10% deadhearts or >2% white ears emerging with widespread tiller loss.

Paddy.name: Rice Blast (Pyricularia oryzae / Magnaporthe oryzae)
Paddy.description: Devastating fungal disease affecting leaves, nodes, and panicle neck resulting in spindle-shaped lesions and broken necks.
symptoms: Spindle-shaped (elliptical) spots on leaves with gray centers and dark brownish margins
Spots coalesce to form large blighted patches causing complete leaf drying
'Neck blast' - blackening and rotting of panicle neck causing complete grain chaffiness
Panicles break and droop at the neck node
risk_conditions: Intermittent drizzles, high relative humidity (>90%), and prolonged leaf wetness (>10 hours)
Cool night temperatures (18–24°C) with heavy morning dew deposition
Excessive nitrogenous fertilization without adequate potassium
monitoring: Inspect lower and middle leaves weekly during seedling and tillering stages for diamond spots
Check boot leaves and emerging panicle necks daily during heading stage under cloudy weather
Monitor disease progression on susceptible border varieties
prevention: Treat seed with Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma viride before nursery sowing
Plant resistant or tolerant certified cultivars recommended for your agro-climatic zone
Apply balanced N:P:K with split potash application to enhance silica deposition in epidermal walls
cultural_control: Burn or compost infected straw and weed hosts (e.g. Echinochloa crus-galli) along bunds
Avoid late transplanting that exposes the heading stage to cool dew-laden weather
Maintain thin water layer; avoid acute moisture stress followed by sudden flooding
mechanical_control: Clean irrigation bunds of wild grasses and collateral hosts that maintain inoculum
Roguing and burning of severely blighted nursery patches
biological_control: Pseudomonas fluorescens foliar spray during tillering and pre-booting stages
Bacillus subtilis biological suspension applications

active_ingredients: Tricyclazole (approved specifically for blast management under official guidelines)
Isoprothiolane / Kasugamycin (as per local university recommendations)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy at initial diamond-spot detection, and panicle neck at 5% heading
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate protective spray if spindle lesions appear on upper leaves before panicle emergence.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Time protective neck blast application precisely at 5% panicle emergence. Strictly follow maximum residue limits (MRL) and harvest intervals.

severity_levels.description: Few scattered spindle-shaped spots on lower leaves; no neck infection.
Coalescing spots on 15–25% of leaf area; early leaf drying observed.
Severe foliar blighting and neck blast observed with breaking panicles.

Paddy.name: Bacterial Leaf Blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae)
Paddy.description: Vascular bacterial disease causing wavy marginal leaf drying from tips downward and 'kresek' wilting in young seedlings.
symptoms: Water-soaked stripes starting from leaf margins near the tip, progressing downwards in wavy patterns
Lesions turn straw-yellow to bleached white with undulating margins
Bacterial ooze droplets (amber-colored beads) on infected leaves in early morning dew
'Kresek' (seedling wilt) where whole hills wilt and die 2–4 weeks after transplanting
risk_conditions: Cyclonic storms, strong winds, and heavy rainfall causing leaf micro-abrasions
Deep submergence of fields with flooded irrigation water transmitting bacteria
Excessive nitrogen fertilizer use creating lush, soft succulent foliage
monitoring: Check leaf tips and upper margins across fields weekly after heavy rain or windy weather
Perform bacterial ooze test in a transparent glass cup with clear water
Survey field corners receiving entry irrigation water from upstream plots
prevention: Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens or approved bactericide formulations
Avoid clipping seedling leaves when transplanting under high disease endemicity zones
Grow resistant varieties carrying robust multi-gene resistance (e.g. Xa21-derived lines)
cultural_control: Drain standing water completely from the field and dry the soil for 3–5 days to arrest spread
Withhold nitrogen top-dressing immediately upon noticing water-soaked margins
Apply extra potassium muriate of potash to strengthen cell wall thickness and lignification
mechanical_control: Isolate field irrigation channels to prevent water flow from infected to healthy plots
Keep field bunds free of weed hosts like Leersia hexandra
biological_control: Pseudomonas fluorescens foliar spray blended with organic carrier
Bacillus amyloliquefaciens microbial antagonist sprays

active_ingredients: Copper hydroxide / Copper oxychloride + Streptomycin-based formulations where officially approved
Fresh cow dung water extract foliar spray (20% filtered supernatant, proven traditional barrier)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy at initial appearance of marginal water-soaked lesions
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Apply protective copper/bactericide drench only at the initial symptom onset; drain field first.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Avoid broad-spectrum chemical overuse which disrupts natural phyllosphere microflora. Adhere strictly to authorized product labels.

severity_levels.description: Less than 5% leaf tips show yellow wavy margins; no kresek wilt.
Marginal drying extending to 15–30% leaf length on multiple tillers.
Severe blighting across entire canopy with extensive leaf scorching and kresek.

Groundnut.name: Groundnut Leaf Miner (Aproaerema modicella)
Groundnut.description: Oligophagous caterpillar mining inside leaflets and later webbing leaves together to feed internally, turning leaves brown.
symptoms: Small brownish blister-like mines on tender leaves visible on upper surface
Webbed leaflets tied together with silk, skeletonized from within
Burnt or scorched appearance of the field during severe infestation
Tiny greenish-brown caterpillars found inside folded or webbed leaflets
risk_conditions: Prolonged dry spells following rain or warm dry weather with high daytime temperatures
Continuous monocropping of groundnut or soyabean in adjacent plots
Moisture stress during vegetative and flowering stages
monitoring: Examine 20 plants randomly per acre weekly for mining blisters and leaflet webs
Install light traps to observe small brownish adult moth emergence
ETL: 5 active larvae per plant or 20% plants showing leaf webbing
prevention: Intercrop groundnut with pearl millet (bajra) or cowpea in 4:1 ratio
Sow trap crops like soyabean on field borders to attract and manage ovipositing moths
Ensure optimal irrigation during critical vegetative and flowering stages
cultural_control: Provide protective irrigation during dry spells to stimulate crop growth and drown soil pupae
Rotate groundnut with non-leguminous cereals such as sorghum, pearl millet, or maize
Destroy wild legume weed hosts around field margins
mechanical_control: Crush webbed leaves between fingers in small plots to kill larvae inside
Set up light traps (1 trap/acre) between 7:00 PM and 10:00 PM to capture adult moths
biological_control: Conservation of eulophid and braconid larval parasitoids (Goniozus spp., Bracon spp.)
Foliar spray of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or Beauveria bassiana on young larvae

active_ingredients: Neem oil / Azadirachtin formulations
Selective approved larvicide (e.g. Chlorantraniliprole or Quinalphos as per TNAU/ICAR guidelines)
chemical_control.target: Young mining larvae before leaves become heavily webbed and protected
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate treatment only if active larval count exceeds 5 per plant or leaf webbing crosses 20%.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Spray late in the evening to protect pollinating honeybees. Adhere strictly to approved local labels and safety intervals.

severity_levels.description: Isolated blister mines on lower leaves; under 5% leaflets affected.
Webbed leaves on 10–20% plants; noticeable larval feeding.
Over 25% foliage skeletonized with general scorched field appearance.

Groundnut.name: Tikka Leaf Spot / Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora arachidicola / Phaeoisariopsis personata)
Groundnut.description: Prevalent fungal disease causing circular dark brown to black spots with yellow halos, causing extensive premature defoliation.
symptoms: Early leaf spot: Circular reddish-brown spots with prominent bright yellow halo on upper leaf surface
Late leaf spot: Dark brown to carbon-black circular spots on lower leaf surface with faint or no halo
Coalescing spots causing premature drying, yellowing, and severe leaflet drop
Elongated dark lesions on petioles, stems, and peg insertions
risk_conditions: Prolonged high relative humidity (>85%) with frequent light showers or heavy night dews
Temperatures between 24°C and 30°C
Low soil organic carbon and potassium deficiencies predisposing leaves to infection
monitoring: Inspect lower canopy leaves weekly beginning 30 days after sowing
Look for tiny circular specks on lower leaf surfaces after morning dew dries
Monitor defoliation rate on lower nodes as an indicator of disease momentum
prevention: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride or approved protective fungicide
Collect and destroy previous crop infected haulms and residues
Follow crop rotation with cereals like sorghum or pearl millet for at least 2 seasons
cultural_control: Ensure wide plant spacing to improve canopy ventilation and reduce humidity build-up
Apply balanced potash fertilization to increase leaf tissue resistance
Remove self-sown groundnut seedlings and weed hosts along boundaries
mechanical_control: Hand-pull and destroy the earliest blighted lower leaves in small seed production plots
Deep summer ploughing to bury fungal conidia present on surface stubble
biological_control: Foliar spray of Pseudomonas fluorescens at 15-day intervals starting 40 days after sowing
Trichoderma harzianum foliar formulations applied during cloudy, humid weather

active_ingredients: Mancozeb (protective contact fungicide)
Carbendazim / Tebuconazole (where recommended under university IPM protocols)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy at initial appearance of circular spots on lower leaves
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate foliar protection when spots first appear on lower canopy and humid weather is forecast.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Alternate between contact and systemic chemistry to prevent fungal resistance development. Follow pre-harvest intervals.

severity_levels.description: Few scattered dark spots on bottom-most leaves; no defoliation.
Spots spreading to middle canopy; 10–20% lower leaf drop observed.
Extensive defoliation; only top young leaves remain green with stem lesions.

Tomato.name: Tomato Fruit Borer (Helicoverpa armigera)
Tomato.description: Voracious caterpillar pest that feeds on flowers and bores circular holes into green and ripe fruits, feeding with its body half outside.
symptoms: Clean, circular entry holes bored into green, developing, and ripe fruits
Internal fruit rot caused by secondary saprophytes entering bore holes
Premature drop of damaged fruits and flower buds
Stout greenish, brownish, or yellowish striped caterpillars feeding on fruit clusters
risk_conditions: Warm, humid conditions during flowering and fruit set
Presence of alternative hosts like maize, chickpea, cotton, or marigold nearby
Continuous tomato cultivation without crop rotation
monitoring: Install Helicoverpa pheromone traps (5 traps/acre) to monitor adult male moth flight peaks
Inspect 20 plants weekly for spherical yellowish-white eggs on tender leaves and flowers
ETL: 1 larva per plant or 5% damaged fruits across sampled clusters
prevention: Plant African marigold (Tagetes erecta) as a trap crop (1 row of marigold for every 16 rows of tomato)
Deep summer ploughing to expose pupae in the soil to predatory birds and intense solar heat
Raise barrier crops of maize or sorghum along field borders
cultural_control: Regular collection and destruction of bored fruits during each picking
Hand-picking of large caterpillars during early morning scouting
Maintain clean field boundaries free of solanaceous weeds (Datura, Solanum nigrum)
mechanical_control: Install sex pheromone traps at 12 traps/acre for mass trapping of male moths
Erect T-shaped bird perches at 15–20 per acre for natural predation by birds
biological_control: Release Trichogramma pretiosum / chilonis egg parasitoids at weekly intervals
Foliar spray of Helicoverpa Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus (HaNPV) or Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)
Conserve predatory anthocorid bugs, spiders, and Chrysoperla carnea

active_ingredients: Azadirachtin (Neem seed kernel extract 5%)
Spinosad / Chlorantraniliprole / Indoxacarb (as approved by CIBRC/TNAU for tomato fruit borer)
chemical_control.target: Newly hatched young larvae before they penetrate the internal fruit cavity
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Spray when egg laying peaks or when larval count crosses 1 caterpillar per plant.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Adhere strictly to waiting periods before fruit harvesting. Rotate chemical modes of action to prevent insecticide resistance.

severity_levels.description: Isolated bored fruits (<3% fruit damage); low trap catches.
3% to 8% fruits damaged; larvae active in flower clusters.
Over 10% fruit damage with extensive rot and high caterpillar population.

Tomato.name: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
Tomato.description: Common fungal disease causing characteristic 'target-board' concentric ring lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit calyx.
symptoms: Small brownish-black spots on older leaves displaying concentric rings (target-board appearance)
Surrounding leaf tissue turns yellow, dries, and drops prematurely
Dark sunken spots with concentric rings at the stem end of fruits
Canopy thins from the ground upwards, exposing green fruits to sunscald
risk_conditions: High humidity (>80%) with alternating warm dry days and wet dewy nights
Crops under nutrient stress (particularly low nitrogen and potassium)
Dense planting with poor airflow and overhead sprinkler irrigation splashing spores
monitoring: Examine lower crown leaves weekly for dark circular target-spots
Monitor disease spread after heavy dew or rainy spells
Check stem bases and fruit calyxes for dark leathery lesions
prevention: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride or approved fungicide before nursery sowing
Mulch soil around plants with straw or plastic film to prevent soil-splash of fungal spores
Stake plants and prune bottom 15–20 cm leaves to eliminate ground contact
cultural_control: Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers to keep leaf canopy dry
Remove and burn blighted lower leaves during staking and pruning operations
Maintain 2–3 year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (cereals, legumes)
mechanical_control: Pruning and disposal of lowest infected leaves touching the soil
Ensure adequate plant and row spacing for cross-ventilation
biological_control: Foliar application of Pseudomonas fluorescens or Bacillus subtilis
Trichoderma harzianum root drench and foliar biological spray

active_ingredients: Mancozeb / Copper oxychloride (protective contact fungicides)
Azoxystrobin / Difenoconazole (systemic fungicides under approved university recommendations)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy upon initial detection of concentric spots on lower leaves
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate protective spray at the first sign of concentric leaf spots during humid weather.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Ensure thorough coverage of both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Respect pre-harvest intervals for edible tomatoes.

severity_levels.description: Isolated concentric spots on bottom leaves; canopy green and dense.
Target-board spots spreading to mid-canopy; 15–25% lower leaf drop.
Severe defoliation with fruit stem-end lesions and extensive sunscald.

Tomato.name: Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV / ToLCV)
Tomato.description: Viral disease transmitted by whiteflies causing extreme leaf curling, stunted growth, puckering, and bushy appearance with no fruit setting.
symptoms: Upward curling, twisting, and puckering of young leaves
Severe stunting of the plant with shortened internodes giving a bushy appearance
Chlorosis and pale yellowing of leaf margins and interveinal areas
Flower drop and failure of fruits to develop or set
risk_conditions: High population of whitefly vectors (Bemisia tabaci) during hot, dry spells
Tomato crops planted adjacent to old infested fields or cotton crops
Presence of infected weed reservoirs (Parthenium, Datura, Abutilon)
monitoring: Install yellow sticky traps (15–20 traps/acre) to monitor whitefly vector flights
Check undersides of young apical leaves in early morning for whitefly adults and nymphs
Inspect field borders for early stunting or yellow leaf margins
prevention: Grow virus-tolerant or resistant tomato hybrids recommended by ICAR/TNAU
Raise tomato nursery under 40-mesh insect-proof nylon net covers
Erect tall border crops like maize, sorghum, or pearl millet (3–4 rows) around the field as physical barriers
cultural_control: Rogue out and destroy virus-infected plants immediately in plastic bags to avoid whitefly escape
Eradicate weed hosts (Parthenium hysterophorus, Datura) within and around the field
Avoid planting overlapping sequential tomato crops
mechanical_control: Erect yellow sticky cards at canopy height to capture adult whitefly vectors
Cover seedling beds with reflective silver-colored plastic mulch to repel whiteflies
biological_control: Conserve predatory mirid bugs (Nesidiocoris tenuis), coccinellid beetles, and lacewings
Foliar application of entomopathogenic fungus Verticillium lecanii / Beauveria bassiana targeting whitefly nymphs

active_ingredients: Neem oil / Azadirachtin formulations targeting whitefly nymphs
Approved systemic vector management products (e.g. Acetamiprid, Diafenthiuron as per CIBRC labels)
chemical_control.target: Whitefly vectors on leaf undersides during early vegetative and transplanting stages
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Target whitefly vectors early if trap catches exceed 5 whiteflies per card per day.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Viruses cannot be cured with chemicals once plants are infected; management is strictly directed at whitefly vector control. Follow label instructions.

severity_levels.description: Isolated curled plants (<2%); low whitefly population on traps.
5% to 10% stunted plants with noticeable curling; moderate whiteflies.
Over 20% plants stunted and bushy; widespread flower shedding.

Cotton.name: Pink Bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella)
Cotton.description: Internal feeder where larvae bore into flower buds and green bolls, causing rosetted flowers and stained lint.
symptoms: 'Rosetted flowers' - twisted flower petals that fail to open fully due to larval webbing
Premature drop of infested flower buds (squares) and young green bolls
Tiny entry holes on green bolls that heal and become invisible, but internal lint and seeds are destroyed
Stained, discolored lint with broken seeds upon boll bursting; pinkish larvae visible inside seeds
risk_conditions: Late-sown crops and ratoon cotton crops extending host availability
Presence of uncleaned ginning waste or cotton seed storage near fields
Cloudy, humid weather during flowering and boll formation stages
monitoring: Install delta / sleeve pheromone traps with gossyplure at 5 traps/acre beginning 45 days after sowing
Dissect 20 green bolls (approx. 20–25 days old) weekly to check for internal burrowing and pink larvae
ETL: 8 moths per trap per day for 3 consecutive days OR 10% damaged green bolls / rosetted flowers
prevention: Adopt synchronous timely sowing within a defined regional planting window
Grow non-transgenic non-Bt cotton refuge lines if growing Bt hybrids as per regulatory rules
Terminate the cotton crop within 150–160 days; strictly avoid ratoon cropping
cultural_control: Hand-pick and destroy rosetted flowers along with the caterpillars inside
Post-harvest grazing of sheep/goats to consume leftover green bolls, followed by deep shredding
Deep summer ploughing to destroy overwintering diapausing larvae in soil and crop debris
mechanical_control: Mass trapping using pheromone traps (10–15 traps/acre) with periodic lure replacement
Install light traps to capture adult nocturnal moths during active flight periods
biological_control: Release Trichogramma bactrae egg parasitoids at weekly intervals
Conserve green lacewings (Chrysoperla carnea) and predatory spiders in the crop canopy

active_ingredients: Neem seed kernel extract / Azadirachtin formulations
Approved selective bollworm chemistry (e.g. Chlorantraniliprole, Emamectin benzoate as per official CIBRC guidance)
chemical_control.target: Newly hatched young larvae on squares and tender bolls before they bore internally
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Apply intervention only when pheromone catches or boll damage crosses official ETL.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Once larvae enter green bolls, chemical efficacy drops dramatically. Adhere strictly to authorized product labels and personal protective equipment standards.

severity_levels.description: Fewer than 5% rosetted flowers; trap catches below threshold.
5% to 10% green bolls show internal larval presence; steady trap catches.
Over 15% green bolls infested with extensive lint staining and seed destruction.

Cotton.name: Bacterial Blight / Black Arm (Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum)
Cotton.description: Multi-phase bacterial disease causing angular leaf spots, black arm cankers on branches, and boll rot.
symptoms: Angular, water-soaked spots on leaves bounded by leaf veinlets, later turning dark brown to black
'Vein blight' - blackening of primary and secondary leaf veins causing leaf blighting
'Black arm' - deep, elongated black cankers on branches and main stem, causing branch snapping
Water-soaked circular spots on bolls turning into sunken dark brown lesions causing boll rotting
risk_conditions: Frequent monsoon showers accompanied by driving winds and high relative humidity (>85%)
Temperatures between 28°C and 34°C
Overhead irrigation or splash dispersal spreading bacterial cells from plant to plant
monitoring: Inspect seedling cotyledons for water-soaked angular spots 2–3 weeks after emergence
Check leaves and branches after stormy rains for angular lesions and stem blackening
Observe green bolls for water-soaked circular lesions
prevention: Acid delinting of cotton seed followed by certified seed treatment with approved bactericides
Cultivate resistant/tolerant cultivars recommended by agricultural universities
Deep ploughing to bury crop residue and eliminate volunteer cotton seedlings
cultural_control: Collect and burn infected plant debris and fallen leaves after harvest
Avoid dense planting; maintain adequate spacing to promote rapid canopy drying
Avoid excessive nitrogenous fertilization; balance with adequate potassium
mechanical_control: Prune and dispose of black-arm-affected lateral branches in seed plots
Field drainage to prevent water stagnation in cotton rows
biological_control: Seed treatment and foliar spray of Pseudomonas fluorescens
Bacillus subtilis microbial biological formulations

active_ingredients: Copper oxychloride + Streptomycin-based formulations (where officially approved for cotton blight)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy and developing branches upon first appearance of angular spots
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate protective spray at the first appearance of angular spots following heavy rainfall.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Avoid spraying during intense midday sunlight to prevent leaf scorch. Strictly follow authorized product labels.

severity_levels.description: Few scattered angular spots on lower leaves; branches clean.
Angular lesions on 15–25% leaf area; minor black streaks on twigs.
Severe black arm lesions with snapping branches and boll rot.

Banana.name: Banana Pseudostem Borer (Odoiporus longicollis)
Banana.description: Destructive weevil borer where grubs tunnel inside the pseudostem causing internal rotting, vascular blockage, and snapping of pseudostems.
symptoms: Small pinhead-sized holes on the pseudostem with transparent or brownish gummy exudation
Yellowing and premature drying of outer leaves starting from the leaf tips
Extensive internal tunneling in pseudostem core filled with rotting larval frass
Pseudostem becomes hollow and snaps under light wind or fruit bunch weight
risk_conditions: Uncleaned plantations with dry leaf sheaths and decaying harvested stumps left in place
Continuous banana cultivation without sanitizing suckers before planting
Warm, humid coastal and river basin climates (temperature 25–32°C)
monitoring: Inspect pseudostems weekly from the 5th month of planting onwards for gummy exudates
Set up longitudinal split pseudostem traps (25–30 traps/acre) baited with fermented juice
Tap pseudostems to check for hollow thudding sounds indicating internal tunneling
prevention: Use tissue-cultured planting material or select suckers exclusively from uninfested mother plantations
Pair suckers thoroughly: peel outer root sheath and dip in biological culture or approved disinfectant
Maintain strict field sanitation by de-trashing dry and hanging leaf sheaths every month
cultural_control: Destroy and chop harvested pseudostems down to ground level and cover with soil
Uproot and destroy severely infested, hollowed pseudostems to prevent weevil multiplication
Clean plantation basins and maintain weed-free soil collars
mechanical_control: Deploy split pseudostem traps (cut stem pieces 50 cm long placed cut-side down on soil) to collect and kill adult weevils
Install pheromone traps (Cosmolure / Odoilure) at 4–5 traps per acre
biological_control: Stem swab or injection of entomopathogenic fungus Beauveria bassiana or Metarhizium anisopliae
Application of entomopathogenic nematodes (Steinernema carpocapsae) around leaf axils

active_ingredients: Neem formulation stem injection or leaf axil application
Approved systemic insecticide stem application (as per TNAU/ICAR crop production guide)
chemical_control.target: Leaf axils and pseudostem bore holes before grubs penetrate the inner central core
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Consider targeted stem injection or axil treatment when bore holes and gummy exudate appear on >5% of plants.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Do not inject or treat pseudostems within 45 days of bunch harvest. Follow local agricultural university guidelines.

severity_levels.description: 1–2 isolated bore holes with slight gumming; canopy green and upright.
Multiple bore holes with heavy gum exudate; outer leaf yellowing on 10–20% plants.
Severe internal hollow tunneling; pseudostem breakage under wind or fruit load.

Banana.name: Panama Wilt / Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense)
Banana.description: Lethal vascular wilt pathogen entering through roots and blocking xylem vessels, causing leaf collapse and plant death.
symptoms: Prominent yellowing of the lower, older leaf margins progressing inward
Leaves buckle and collapse at the petiole junction, hanging down like a skirt around the pseudostem
Longitudinal splitting of the pseudostem base near the ground line
Characteristic dark red, purple, or black vascular discoloration seen in cross-section of pseudostem
risk_conditions: Planting in fields with historical Fusarium wilt infestation (chlamydospores survive >20 years)
Waterlogging, poor drainage, or nematode root injury predisposing roots to infection
Using uncertified suckers sourced from wilt-infected orchards
monitoring: Survey plantation monthly for characteristic lower leaf collapse and petiole buckling
Examine base of pseudostem for longitudinal splits
Cut discarded sucker cross-sections to verify vascular ring discoloration
prevention: Plant certified tissue culture plantlets or wilt-resistant varieties (e.g. resistant Cavendish strains)
Apply lime or dolomite to acidic soils to raise pH above 6.5, which suppresses Fusarium virulence
Incorporate organic compost fortified heavily with Trichoderma viride at planting
cultural_control: Strict quarantine: do not move suckers, soil, or pruning implements from infected fields
Uproot and burn diseased plants along with the rhizome inside the pit; treat the pit with lime
Rotate with wetland paddy for 1–2 years to submerge soil and reduce fungal inoculum load
mechanical_control: Sterilize cutting machetes and knives with 10% bleach or flame between individual plants
Dig isolation trenches around infected mats to prevent root-to-root transmission
biological_control: Soil application of Trichoderma viride / T. harzianum blended with neem cake in planting pits
Pseudomonas fluorescens sucker dipping and root-zone drenching

chemical_control.target: N/A - Vascular Fusarium wilt cannot be effectively cured chemically once established.
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Chemical foliar sprays are ineffective against vascular Panama wilt.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Use only locally approved soil sanitization or biological management. Never rely on chemical sprays to cure wilted plants.

severity_levels.description: Yellowing on outer margins of 1–2 bottom leaves on isolated plants.
Buckling of multiple leaf petioles; longitudinal splitting at stem base.
Complete leaf skirt collapse, severe vascular browning, and plant death across mats.

Chilli.name: Chilli Thrips (Scirtothrips dorsalis)
Chilli.description: Slender rasping-sucking pest causing leaves to curl upward ('boat-shaped'), turn brittle, and develop silvery-bronze underside patches.
symptoms: Upward curling of leaf margins into a boat-like or cup-like shape
Crinkling, thickening, and brittleness of tender young leaves
Silvery or bronzed patches on the undersides of leaves and linear scabby scars on fruits
Stunted crop growth with drop of flowers and deformed small fruits
risk_conditions: Dry, warm weather with low relative humidity and absence of rain showers
Excessive use of nitrogenous fertilizers producing tender succulent growth
Continuous sole cropping of chilli without border barriers
monitoring: Tap terminal shoots over a white sheet of paper or plastic board to count tiny yellowish thrips
Install blue or yellow sticky traps at canopy level (15–20 traps/acre)
ETL: 2 thrips per tender leaf or leaf curl symptoms on 10% of plants
prevention: Raise barrier crops of maize or sorghum (2–3 border rows) to impede thrips movement
Intercrop with marigold, cowpea, or coriander to encourage beneficial predatory insects
Maintain overhead sprinkler irrigation occasionally during dry spells to wash thrips off foliage
cultural_control: Avoid continuous monocropping; rotate with non-host crops like cereals or legumes
Keep field bunds clear of weeds like Parthenium hysterophorus and Achyranthes aspera
Apply balanced fertilizers and avoid surplus nitrogen top-dressings
mechanical_control: Install blue sticky traps (proven higher attraction for thrips than yellow) at canopy level
Use reflective silver mulch in seedling beds to disorient incoming thrips
biological_control: Conservation of predatory anthocorid bugs (Orius spp.) and phytoseiid predatory mites
Foliar application of entomopathogenic fungus Lecanicillium lecanii / Beauveria bassiana

active_ingredients: Neem oil / Azadirachtin formulations
Approved selective chemistry (e.g. Spinosad, Fipronil, Diafenthiuron as per CIBRC labels)
chemical_control.target: Tender foliage undersides and terminal growing points during early morning or late afternoon
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Spray when counts exceed 2 thrips per leaf or early upward cupping begins on tender flush.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Rotate insecticide modes of action to prevent rapid thrips resistance. Adhere strictly to pre-harvest intervals for green and red dry chillies.

severity_levels.description: Slight upward curling on few shoot tips; under 2 thrips per leaf.
Upward boat-shaped cupping on 10–25% foliage; noticeable bronzing on leaf undersides.
Severe curling, leaf brittleness, stunted growth, and distorted small fruits.

Chilli.name: Anthracnose & Fruit Rot / Die-Back (Colletotrichum capsici)
Chilli.description: Major fungal disease causing circular sunken lesions with concentric rings of black acervuli on ripe fruits, and twig die-back.
symptoms: Circular or elliptical sunken lesions on developing and ripe fruits with concentric black rings
Diseased fruits turn straw-colored to bleached white, shrivel, and drop prematurely
'Die-back' - tender twigs dry and wither from tip downwards, turning white to grayish-brown
Tiny black dot-like fungal fruiting bodies (acervuli) visible inside fruit lesions
risk_conditions: High relative humidity (>80%) with warm temperatures (28–32°C) and cloudy days
Intermittent rains during fruit ripening and maturity stages
Dense plant canopy with stagnant air and poor drainage
monitoring: Inspect ripening fruits and green fruit clusters weekly for water-soaked sunken specks
Check upper branch tips for downward drying (die-back)
Monitor disease after sudden unseasonal showers during harvesting phase
prevention: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride or approved protective fungicide
Collect seeds exclusively from certified disease-free ripe fruits
Follow wide plant spacing (60 x 45 cm or 75 x 60 cm) to facilitate canopy aeration
cultural_control: Prompt collection and burning of rotten and dropped fruits during each picking round
Prune and burn die-back-affected twigs cutting 2–3 cm into healthy tissue
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation during the flowering and fruit ripening stages
mechanical_control: Hand-pick spotted fruits early before fungal spores produce black acervuli rings
Ensure field drainage channels rapidly evacuate excess rain runoff
biological_control: Foliar spray of Pseudomonas fluorescens at 15-day intervals from flowering stage
Trichoderma harzianum foliar application during humid periods

active_ingredients: Copper oxychloride / Mancozeb (protective contact fungicides)
Azoxystrobin / Difenoconazole / Tebuconazole (where recommended by university IPM guidelines)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy and fruit clusters at initial spotting or during sudden overcast rain spells
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate foliar protection at the onset of flowering and repeat if wet weather coincides with fruit ripening.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Avoid spraying close to harvest without respecting pre-harvest safety intervals. Alternate chemistries to prevent resistance.

severity_levels.description: Isolated small sunken spots on <3% fruits; twig dieback absent.
Sunken lesions on 5–15% ripening fruits; occasional dieback twigs.
Widespread fruit rotting with black acervuli rings and extensive branch die-back.

Maize.name: Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda)
Maize.description: Invasive, highly destructive noctuid caterpillar that feeds deep within the leaf whorl, causing ragged 'shot-hole' feeding and ear damage.
symptoms: Elongated pinholes and 'shot-holes' in young whorl leaves developing into large ragged tears
Abundant moist, saw-dust-like golden-brown fecal frass filling the central whorl
Larva displays an inverted white 'Y' mark on the dark head and 4 dark spots arranged in a square on the 8th abdominal segment
Direct boring into developing tassels and corn ear cobs
risk_conditions: Staggered planting of maize in adjacent fields creating continuous vegetative host availability
Warm weather (25–30°C) with intermittent dry spells and light showers
Monoculture of sweet corn or fodder maize without refuge or trap crops
monitoring: Scout field in a 'W' or zigzag pattern examining 20 consecutive plants in 5 locations weekly
Install pheromone traps with FAW lure (5 traps/acre) to detect early male moth activity
ETL: 5% damaged plants at seedling stage; 10% damaged plants at mid-whorl (V4–V8) stage
prevention: Adopt synchronous community sowing within the recommended local agro-climatic window
Intercrop maize with pulses like cowpea, pigeonpea, or blackgram in 2:1 or 4:1 ratio
Apply neem cake in the soil during final land preparation to suppress pupation
cultural_control: Hand-pick and crush egg masses (covered with yellowish-brown scales) and young caterpillars
Whorl application of dry soil or fine river sand mixed with ash (traditional physical barrier that irritates larvae)
Deep ploughing after harvest to expose pupae in the soil to bird predators and solar heat
mechanical_control: Install pheromone traps (10–15 traps/acre) for mass trapping and monitoring
Erect T-shaped bird perches at 15–20 per acre at early crop stages
biological_control: Release egg parasitoid Trichogramma pretiosum or Telenomus remus
Whorl application of entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium rileyi or Beauveria bassiana
Foliar spray of Spodoptera frugiperda Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus (SfNPV) or Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)

active_ingredients: Neem formulation (Azadirachtin 1500 ppm) for early whorl application
Chlorantraniliprole / Spinetoram / Emamectin benzoate (approved by DPPQ&S/ICAR guidelines)
chemical_control.target: Directly into the central leaf whorl where caterpillars hide and feed
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Apply targeted whorl treatment when window pane damage exceeds 10% of plants at early whorl stage.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Direct spray nozzle directly into the leaf whorl for effective contact. Wear PPE and follow CIBRC authorized labels.

severity_levels.description: Pinholes on whorl leaves in <5% plants; minimal fecal frass.
Ragged tears and visible saw-dust frass in 5–15% plants; active caterpillars in whorls.
Over 20% plants severely skeletonized, whorl destruction, and ear cob damage.

Maize.name: Turcicum Leaf Blight / Northern Corn Leaf Blight (Exserohilum turcicum)
Maize.description: Fungal foliar disease causing large, elongated spindle-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions that coalesce to kill entire leaves.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, spindle-shaped lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long) on leaves
Lesions start as grayish-green, turning tan or straw-colored with dark margins
Dark velvety fungal sporulation visible inside lesions under humid morning conditions
Premature drying and burning of the entire foliage from bottom leaves upwards
risk_conditions: Moderate temperatures (18–27°C) accompanied by high relative humidity (>90%)
Heavy dews and frequent overcast cloudy weather during vegetative growth
Continuous maize-on-maize cropping with infected residue remaining on the surface
monitoring: Inspect lower leaves weekly starting at knee-high stage (V6 stage)
Check for elongated grayish streaks after foggy or dewy mornings
Assess percentage of leaf area affected on leaves at and below the ear cob
prevention: Plant certified resistant/tolerant hybrids recommended by ICAR/SAUs
Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride or approved protective fungicide
Deep ploughing to bury crop residue and encourage microbial decomposition of fungal stroma
cultural_control: Rotate maize with non-grass crops like pulses, soybean, or oilseeds
Avoid high plant densities; ensure proper row spacing to enhance airflow and sunlight
Apply balanced NPK fertilization with split potassium application to improve leaf resilience
mechanical_control: Collect and compost or burn infected lower leaves in small seed production plots
Ensure field ditches rapidly evacuate excess surface water after storms
biological_control: Foliar application of Pseudomonas fluorescens or Bacillus subtilis
Trichoderma harzianum foliar biological spray

active_ingredients: Mancozeb (protective contact fungicide)
Azoxystrobin / Pyraclostrobin (where officially recommended under university IPM protocols)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy at initial detection of spindle lesions before ear emergence
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate foliar protection when spindle lesions appear on lower leaves prior to tasseling.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Spray early morning or late evening for thorough coverage. Respect pre-harvest safety intervals for green cob harvest.

severity_levels.description: Few scattered spindle lesions on bottom leaves; ear leaf clean.
Lesions spreading to mid-canopy; 15–25% leaf area affected below ear.
Extensive blighting of upper leaves including the ear leaf; premature drying.

Rice.name: Yellow Stem Borer (Scirpophaga incertulas)
Rice.description: Monophagous pest where larvae bore inside the tillers causing 'deadheart' at vegetative stage and 'white ear' at heading stage.
symptoms: 'Deadheart' - central vegetative shoots dry up and can be pulled out easily with severed base
'White ear' - bleached, empty erect panicles with no grain filling during reproductive stage
Small exit and entrance pinholes on lower stem nodes
Buff-colored egg masses covered with yellowish-brown silky anal hairs on upper leaf tips
risk_conditions: High nitrogen fertilizer application exceeding recommended doses
Staggered planting across adjacent fields creating continuous host presence
Warm, humid weather with overcast skies and high night temperatures
monitoring: Scout 20 hill clusters diagonally across the field twice a week
Install light traps (1 trap/acre) and sex pheromone traps (3–4 traps/acre) to monitor moth flights
Economic Threshold Level (ETL): 1 egg mass/sq.m or 2 moths/trap/day or 10% deadhearts / 2% white ears
prevention: Synchronous community transplanting across contiguous field blocks
Clip leaf tips of seedlings before transplanting to eliminate attached egg masses
Adopt balanced nitrogen application split into 3–4 timings rather than heavy basal doses
cultural_control: Harvest rice plants at ground level and plough stubbles immediately to expose diapausing larvae
Alternate wetting and moderate drying irrigation rather than continuous deep flooding
Allow predatory ducks or birds into fields during fallow and early tillering
mechanical_control: Hand-collection and destruction of egg masses from nursery and early transplanted fields
Erect T-shaped bird perches at 15–20 per acre for insectivorous birds like drongos
biological_control: Release egg parasitoid Trichogramma japonicum at weekly intervals starting 30 days after transplanting
Conservation of spiders (Lycosa pseudoannulata), mirid bugs, and carabid ground beetles

active_ingredients: Neem formulation (Azadirachtin)
Cartap hydrochloride / Chlorantraniliprole (where ETL is exceeded under official guidance)
chemical_control.target: Newly hatched young larvae before they bore completely into the interior of the culm
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Apply intervention only when moth catches or deadhearts exceed established Economic Threshold Levels.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Avoid spraying if predator spider population is high. Maintain water level for 24–48 hours post application according to label instructions.

severity_levels.description: Under 5% deadhearts at vegetative stage; isolated egg masses observed.
5% to 10% deadhearts or active pheromone trap catches crossing ETL.
Over 10% deadhearts or >2% white ears emerging with widespread tiller loss.

Rice.name: Rice Blast (Pyricularia oryzae / Magnaporthe oryzae)
Rice.description: Devastating fungal disease affecting leaves, nodes, and panicle neck resulting in spindle-shaped lesions and broken necks.
symptoms: Spindle-shaped (elliptical) spots on leaves with gray centers and dark brownish margins
Spots coalesce to form large blighted patches causing complete leaf drying
'Neck blast' - blackening and rotting of panicle neck causing complete grain chaffiness
Panicles break and droop at the neck node
risk_conditions: Intermittent drizzles, high relative humidity (>90%), and prolonged leaf wetness (>10 hours)
Cool night temperatures (18–24°C) with heavy morning dew deposition
Excessive nitrogenous fertilization without adequate potassium
monitoring: Inspect lower and middle leaves weekly during seedling and tillering stages for diamond spots
Check boot leaves and emerging panicle necks daily during heading stage under cloudy weather
Monitor disease progression on susceptible border varieties
prevention: Treat seed with Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma viride before nursery sowing
Plant resistant or tolerant certified cultivars recommended for your agro-climatic zone
Apply balanced N:P:K with split potash application to enhance silica deposition in epidermal walls
cultural_control: Burn or compost infected straw and weed hosts (e.g. Echinochloa crus-galli) along bunds
Avoid late transplanting that exposes the heading stage to cool dew-laden weather
Maintain thin water layer; avoid acute moisture stress followed by sudden flooding
mechanical_control: Clean irrigation bunds of wild grasses and collateral hosts that maintain inoculum
Roguing and burning of severely blighted nursery patches
biological_control: Pseudomonas fluorescens foliar spray during tillering and pre-booting stages
Bacillus subtilis biological suspension applications

active_ingredients: Tricyclazole (approved specifically for blast management under official guidelines)
Isoprothiolane / Kasugamycin (as per local university recommendations)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy at initial diamond-spot detection, and panicle neck at 5% heading
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate protective spray if spindle lesions appear on upper leaves before panicle emergence.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Time protective neck blast application precisely at 5% panicle emergence. Strictly follow maximum residue limits (MRL) and harvest intervals.

severity_levels.description: Few scattered spindle-shaped spots on lower leaves; no neck infection.
Coalescing spots on 15–25% of leaf area; early leaf drying observed.
Severe foliar blighting and neck blast observed with breaking panicles.

Rice.name: Bacterial Leaf Blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae)
Rice.description: Vascular bacterial disease causing wavy marginal leaf drying from tips downward and 'kresek' wilting in young seedlings.
symptoms: Water-soaked stripes starting from leaf margins near the tip, progressing downwards in wavy patterns
Lesions turn straw-yellow to bleached white with undulating margins
Bacterial ooze droplets (amber-colored beads) on infected leaves in early morning dew
'Kresek' (seedling wilt) where whole hills wilt and die 2–4 weeks after transplanting
risk_conditions: Cyclonic storms, strong winds, and heavy rainfall causing leaf micro-abrasions
Deep submergence of fields with flooded irrigation water transmitting bacteria
Excessive nitrogen fertilizer use creating lush, soft succulent foliage
monitoring: Check leaf tips and upper margins across fields weekly after heavy rain or windy weather
Perform bacterial ooze test in a transparent glass cup with clear water
Survey field corners receiving entry irrigation water from upstream plots
prevention: Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens or approved bactericide formulations
Avoid clipping seedling leaves when transplanting under high disease endemicity zones
Grow resistant varieties carrying robust multi-gene resistance (e.g. Xa21-derived lines)
cultural_control: Drain standing water completely from the field and dry the soil for 3–5 days to arrest spread
Withhold nitrogen top-dressing immediately upon noticing water-soaked margins
Apply extra potassium muriate of potash to strengthen cell wall thickness and lignification
mechanical_control: Isolate field irrigation channels to prevent water flow from infected to healthy plots
Keep field bunds free of weed hosts like Leersia hexandra
biological_control: Pseudomonas fluorescens foliar spray blended with organic carrier
Bacillus amyloliquefaciens microbial antagonist sprays

active_ingredients: Copper hydroxide / Copper oxychloride + Streptomycin-based formulations where officially approved
Fresh cow dung water extract foliar spray (20% filtered supernatant, proven traditional barrier)
chemical_control.target: Foliar canopy at initial appearance of marginal water-soaked lesions
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Apply protective copper/bactericide drench only at the initial symptom onset; drain field first.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Avoid broad-spectrum chemical overuse which disrupts natural phyllosphere microflora. Adhere strictly to authorized product labels.

severity_levels.description: Less than 5% leaf tips show yellow wavy margins; no kresek wilt.
Marginal drying extending to 15–30% leaf length on multiple tillers.
Severe blighting across entire canopy with extensive leaf scorching and kresek.

Sorghum.name: Sorghum Shoot Fly (Atherigona soccata)
Sorghum.description: Major dipteran seedling pest where maggots cut the central growing point, creating deadhearts in 1-4 week old seedlings.
symptoms: Drying and withering of the central shoot (deadheart) in young seedlings
Dead central leaf pulls out easily, giving off a foul rotting odor
Excessive tillering in damaged plants, resulting in weak, unthrifty growth
risk_conditions: Delayed monsoon sowing
Cloudy weather and high humidity during seedling stage
monitoring: Inspect 20 seedlings per quadrant weekly; calculate deadheart percentage
prevention: Sow early with the onset of monsoon
Use higher seed rate (10-12 kg/ha) and thin out affected deadhearts at 15 days
cultural_control: Intercrop sorghum with pulses like red gram or cowpea (2:1 ratio)
Clean weeding and removal of wild grass hosts
mechanical_control: Install fishmeal bait traps (10-12 traps/ha) to capture adult shoot flies
biological_control: Conserve natural parasitoids like Trichogramma chilonis and predatory earwigs

active_ingredients: Neem seed kernel extract 5%
Approved seed treatment or granular soil insecticides as per local extension guide
chemical_control.target: Emerging adult flies and young seedlings within 15 days of sowing
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate control if more than 10% seedlings show central shoot deadhearts.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Follow registered CIBRC product label directions. Avoid spraying in rain.

severity_levels.description: Less than 5% seedlings exhibit shoot fly deadhearts.
5% to 10% seedlings damaged; localized tillering starting.
More than 10% seedlings destroyed with widespread deadheart formation.

Pearl Millet.name: Downy Mildew / Green Ear (Sclerospora graminicola)
Pearl Millet.description: Severe oomycete disease causing systemic chlorosis and transformation of floral earheads into leafy green leafy structures.
symptoms: Pale yellow chlorotic streaks on upper leaves starting from base
White downy fungal growth on lower leaf surfaces under high humidity
Earheads fully or partially transformed into a mass of leafy green twisted structures (green ear symptom)
risk_conditions: Cool nights (15-20°C) with high relative humidity (>85%) during early vegetative growth
monitoring: Scout fields at seedling (20 days) and boot stages for foliar downy streaks and green ears
prevention: Use certified downy mildew resistant hybrids
Rogue out infected chlorotic seedlings at first weeding
cultural_control: Crop rotation with non-host crops (pulses/oilseeds)
Deep summer ploughing to bury oospores
mechanical_control: Rogue and burn green-ear heads before fungal sporangia disperse
biological_control: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens formulations

active_ingredients: Approved systemic fungicide seed treatment or foliar spray as recommended by state agricultural university
chemical_control.target: Foliar downy mildew at early vegetative stage
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Apply foliar treatment if disease incidence exceeds 5% in high-humidity periods.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Follow statutory CIBRC dosage instructions and personal safety measures.

severity_levels.description: Isolated chlorotic plants (<2%) with minimal downy growth.
2% to 5% plants exhibiting foliar streaks and early head deformation.
More than 5% green ear malformation and significant yield loss risk.

Finger Millet.name: Finger Millet Blast (Magnaporthe grisea)
Finger Millet.description: Most destructive fungal disease affecting finger millet leaves, stems, necks, and earhead fingers.
symptoms: Spindle-shaped elliptical lesions with gray centers and dark brown margins on leaves
Black neck lesion causing complete earhead choking and premature chaffy grains (neck blast)
Blackish lesions on individual fingers resulting in grain abortion (finger blast)
risk_conditions: Intermittent rains, cloudy weather, and high relative humidity (>90%) with night temperatures 20-22°C
monitoring: Inspect nursery seedlings and field crop at tillering, flowering, and grain filling stages
prevention: Sow blast-tolerant varieties recommended for your agro-climatic zone
Avoid excessive synthetic nitrogen applications
cultural_control: Maintain proper plant spacing for canopy aeration
Destroy volunteer hosts and wild grasses around field bunds
mechanical_control: Collection and safe disposal of heavily infected blast stubbles
biological_control: Seed bio-priming and foliar spray of Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%)

active_ingredients: Approved triazole or strobilurin fungicides as per local extension guide
chemical_control.target: Leaf and neck blast at early symptom appearance
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Spray when leaf blast lesions appear on more than 5% canopy leaves before head emergence.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Comply with pre-harvest intervals (PHI) and container label recommendations.

severity_levels.description: Isolated spindle spots on lower leaves with no neck infection.
5% to 15% leaf canopy affected; occasional neck blast lesions.
More than 15% leaf infection with widespread neck and finger blast.

Chickpea.name: Gram Pod Borer (Helicoverpa armigera)
Chickpea.description: Polyphagous noctuid caterpillar that defoliates tender leaves and bores clean circular entry holes into green pods.
symptoms: Defoliation and severed flower buds in early reproductive phase
Clean circular holes bored into developing green pods
Caterpillar feeding with anterior half of body inside the pod and posterior half exposed outside
risk_conditions: Warm winter days followed by cool nights
Dense vegetative canopy and cloudy spells during flowering
monitoring: Erect pheromone traps at 5-10 traps/ha; scout 20 plants weekly for egg and larval counts
prevention: Intercrop chickpea with coriander, mustard, or marigold to invite natural predator wasps
Deep summer ploughing to expose pupae
cultural_control: Install bird perches (T-shaped bamboo perches at 50/ha) for insectivorous birds
Hand-pick large larvae during early morning hours
mechanical_control: Pheromone traps for male moth trapping and monitoring threshold triggers
biological_control: Foliar spray of Helicoverpa armigera Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus (HaNPV @ 250 LE/ha)
Conserve larval parasitoids (Campoletis chlorideae) and predatory bugs

active_ingredients: Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE 5%)
CIBRC-approved diamide or spinosad chemistries where ETL is breached
chemical_control.target: Young 1st and 2nd instar larvae before they enter pods
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Intervene if moth catches exceed 5 moths/trap/night or larval count exceeds 1 larva/meter row (ETL).
chemical_control.safety_notes: Do not spray broad-spectrum chemicals during peak bee pollination. Strict adherence to label guidelines.

severity_levels.description: Less than 1 larva per meter row; minimal pod scratching.
1 to 2 larvae per meter row; initial pod entry holes visible.
More than 2 larvae per meter row with extensive pod damage.

Sugarcane.name: Early Shoot Borer (Chilo infuscatellus)
Sugarcane.description: Destructive borer attacking young sugarcane shoots within 1-3 months of planting, creating characteristic deadhearts.
symptoms: Drying and death of the central spindle (deadheart) in 30-100 day old canes
Emits a foul offensive odor upon pulling out the dead central shoot
Bore hole visible at soil level or base of the shoot with sawdust-like frass
risk_conditions: High temperature (>35°C) and low atmospheric humidity during early tillering stage
monitoring: Inspect 100 shoots per row; calculate deadheart percentage at 30, 45, and 60 days
prevention: Plant early in December-January to escape peak shoot borer attack
Trash mulching (3 t/ha) across cane furrows suppresses egg laying
cultural_control: Frequent light irrigations to moderate microclimate temperature
Earthing up along cane rows at 45 days to bury shoot entry points
mechanical_control: Remove and destroy deadheart shoots by cutting below ground level
biological_control: Release egg parasitoid Trichogramma chilonis at 50,000/ha at 10-day intervals
Conservation of predatory earwigs and spiders

active_ingredients: CIBRC registered systemic granular or spray insecticide as per state agricultural university recommendation
chemical_control.target: Early shoot base prior to larval boring
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Initiate control if deadheart incidence exceeds 15% economic threshold level.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Observe safe handling and application guidelines as specified on the registered label.

severity_levels.description: Deadhearts below 5%; minimal tillering impact.
5% to 15% deadhearts; compensatory tillering active.
More than 15% deadhearts with severe shoot mortality.

Brinjal.name: Shoot and Fruit Borer (Leucinodes orbonalis)
Brinjal.description: Key insect pest causing drooping of growing shoots in early stage and boring clean holes filled with frass into fruits.
symptoms: Wilting and drooping of tender terminal shoot tips in young plants
Exit holes plugged with excreta/frass on developing brinjal fruits
Internal fruit pulp rotting and unmarketable distorted fruits
risk_conditions: Continuous warm humid weather and overlapping solanaceous crops
monitoring: Scout plants weekly; install Lucinlure pheromone traps at 12 traps/ha
prevention: Clip and destroy wilted terminal shoots along with larvae weekly
Avoid continuous brinjal monoculture
cultural_control: Intercrop with coriander or fennel to encourage natural parasitoids
Clean cultivation and destruction of crop residues
mechanical_control: Pheromone mass trapping using Lucinlure septa
Manual removal and deep burial of bore-damaged fruits
biological_control: Conserve natural larval parasitoids like Trathala flavo-orbitalis
Foliar application of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or NSKE 5%

active_ingredients: Neem Seed Kernel Extract 5%
CIBRC-registered selective insecticides as per local extension guide
chemical_control.target: Adult moths and young larvae prior to fruit boring
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Spray if fruit damage exceeds 5% or shoot wilting exceeds 1-2 per plant.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Observe mandatory pre-harvest interval (PHI) between spraying and fruit picking. Strictly follow registered label directions.

severity_levels.description: Isolated shoot drooping (<2%); zero fruit damage.
2% to 5% fruit infestation with moderate shoot wilting.
More than 5% fruits bored; heavy frass and unmarketable yield.

Okra.name: Shoot and Fruit Borer (Earias vittella / Earias insulana)
Okra.description: Lepidopteran borer that bores into tender vegetative shoots causing wilting, and enters developing pods making them distorted.
symptoms: Drooping and withering of growing tips in vegetative stage
Bored holes on pods plugged with larval excreta
Distorted, deformed pods with internal seed consumption
risk_conditions: High humidity with warm temperatures and proximity to cotton crops
monitoring: Weekly field scouting of 20 plants; install pheromone traps at 10/ha
prevention: Collect and destroy infested shoots and bored fruits during every harvest picking
Deep summer ploughing
cultural_control: Avoid continuous okra-cotton crop rotation
Grow marigold on borders as a trap and nectar crop
mechanical_control: Install yellow sticky traps and pheromone traps
biological_control: Release Trichogramma chilonis at 50,000/ha
Foliar spray of NSKE 5% at early square and pod formation

active_ingredients: Neem formulations
Approved active ingredients registered by CIBRC for okra borer
chemical_control.target: Young caterpillars before entry into pods
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Spray if fruit infestation crosses 5% threshold level.
chemical_control.safety_notes: Pick tender pods before spraying and respect harvest withholding period. Adhere to product labels.

severity_levels.description: Less than 2% pod damage; isolated shoot drooping.
2% to 5% pod infestation; localized entry holes.
More than 5% pods infested with visible frass and distortion.

Onion.name: Onion Thrips (Thrips tabaci)
Onion.description: Minute rasping-sucking insect feeding between leaf sheaths, creating silvery blotches and predisposing plants to purple blotch disease.
symptoms: Silvery-white patches and streaks on leaves giving foliage a bleached appearance
Curling, twisting, and premature drying of leaf tips
Reduced bulb size and vigor due to impaired chlorophyll photosynthesis
risk_conditions: Dry, hot weather with low humidity (<50%) and absence of rain
monitoring: Inspect 20 random plants weekly by gently pulling inner leaf sheaths apart
prevention: Maintain adequate soil moisture through sprinkler or drip irrigation
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizers
cultural_control: Intercrop onion with barrier crops like maize or barrier grass to reduce thrips movement
Field sanitation and removal of weed hosts
mechanical_control: Erect blue or yellow sticky traps at 25-30 traps/ha
biological_control: Foliar application of entomopathogenic fungus Beauveria bassiana or Verticillium lecanii
Conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius spp.) and ladybird beetles

active_ingredients: Neem seed extract / Azadirachtin
CIBRC-registered contact/systemic insecticide for onion thrips
chemical_control.target: Nymphs and adults concealed within inner leaf sheaths
chemical_control.consideration_criteria: Treat when population exceeds 15-20 thrips per plant (ETL).
chemical_control.safety_notes: Use wetting agent for waxy onion foliage. Follow registered label and local extension guidelines.

severity_levels.description: Fewer than 10 thrips per plant; faint silvery specks.
10 to 25 thrips per plant; distinct silvery patches on foliage.
More than 25 thrips per plant; severe leaf blighting and tip curling.
